Charles Rangel. A Long Island politician and longtime Harlem congressman who chaired the House Ways and Means Committee, overseeing United States tax and trade policy. A Korean War veteran and consummate insider, he accumulated legislative seniority and power across five decades.

Rangel was elected to the House from Harlem in 1970 and served forty-six consecutive years until 2017, making him one of the longest-serving members in congressional history. From 2007 to 2011, he became the first Black chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee, the most powerful fiscal committee in the House, controlling tax and tariff legislation. His military service as a decorated Korean War veteran shaped his commitment to veterans' benefits and labor protections.

Rangel championed the Earned Income Tax Credit, an anti-poverty program that became one of the largest federal social-welfare initiatives. He was known for constituent service and political machine-building in Harlem, navigating ethics investigations in the 2010s without losing his seat. Throughout his career, he mentored younger Black legislators and served as a bridge between old-guard civil rights politicians and post-movement Democratic leadership, following in the footsteps of his predecessor Adam Clayton Powell Jr.
